body.text: Intelligence professionals carry an unrecognised ethical responsibility. It arises when they shape what political decision-makers come to know, which risks are held to be salient, and which options appear available.

Intelligence ethics is still too often framed around formal authority and the final decision-making, both of which reside with ministers. But intelligence professionals exert significant influence in the process through collection, analysis, framing, prioritisation and the communication of uncertainty.
Intelligence organisations need to understand this ethical responsibility and translate it into governance improvements, leadership expectations and professional practice.
Three examples of official actions can illustrate how they carry unrecognised ethical responsibilities.

First, priorities assigned in collecting intelligence will shape the problem that ministers see. Suppose Australia is concerned about growing foreign influence in a Pacific state. Officials choose to concentrate intelligence collection on military access and security cooperation, giving less attention to such matters as political financing, debt exposure and technology dependence. So the picture that ministers get is dominated by the possibility of a future military foothold, rather than by broader political and economic leverage. Security responses may then appear more urgent than economic or diplomatic ones.

Second, strategic warning can shape when government believes action is necessary. Intelligence may, for example, have tracked growing foreign control over telecommunications, ports and digital infrastructure across the region. Intelligence leaders assess that the pattern now amounts to an emerging strategic dependency in the region rather than a series of largely unrelated and uncoordinated commercial investments.
Once intelligence professionals report their perception of a pattern to ministers, intervention may appear necessary, whereas the situation may in fact require only continued monitoring.

Third, intelligence advice can shape ministers’ understanding of which responses remain credible. A friendly neighbouring country may, for example, begin deepening security cooperation with a strategic competitor of Australia. Intelligence officials judge the cooperation to be significant, but its intent remains ambiguous: it may represent new alignment by the friend, an attempt at hedging, or simply an effort by it and Australia’s competitor to gain concessions from each other.

If intelligence advice gives greater weight to strategic alignment, ministers may conclude the right response is to put pressure on the friend or reduce cooperation. If the advice gives greater weight to hedging and the friend’s autonomy, continued engagement may remain credible. In either case, ministers will make the decision, but intelligence professionals will have helped define the range of choices government sees as reasonable.
Intelligence organisations should recognise this influence as an ethical responsibility and build it into how they lead and train intelligence officers and review their work.

Doing so would not transfer responsibility for policy to intelligence professionals. Ministers must remain accountable for the decisions they make. But ministerial authority should not erase responsibility for choices made earlier in the process.

Intelligence organisations already have strong standards for sourcing, analysis, uncertainty and the quality of assessments. Those safeguards are essential. But they do not always ask how choices made during the intelligence process may shape the decisions that follow.

Improved governance should make that influence easier to see. Reviews of major collection priorities, strategic warnings and important assessments should consider not only whether the work is sound, but what has been prioritised, what has received less attention and how those choices may affect what ministers see.

Leadership matters for the same reason. Senior officials should challenge the assumptions behind warnings and assessments, ask what would change the judgement and consider whether other credible interpretations have been given proper weight. Strategic warnings should be tested carefully, because elevating an issue can itself change how urgently ministers perceive it.

None of this requires intelligence professionals to give every interpretation equal weight. Good intelligence should narrow uncertainty when the evidence supports doing so. But when judgement substantially narrows the choices presented to government, those making or endorsing it should understand the significance of that influence.

Professional development should reflect this responsibility. Intelligence professionals are trained to assess sources, handle uncertainty and communicate confidence. They should also be prepared to recognise when decisions about collection, warning or presentation are changing the way a problem will be understood by others.

Responsibility should follow influence, not simply an official’s rank. An intelligence organisation’s leaders will often carry the greatest responsibility, because they decide what reaches ministers, how urgently it is presented and which competing views receive attention. But influence can also sit with specialists, collectors or others whose expertise becomes central to a particular decision.

Responsibility for influence is not the same as responsibility for the eventual outcome. Contributing work to a minister’s policy decision does not make an intelligence professional responsible for it. But nor does the minister’s authority remove responsibility for choices made on the way to that decision. Formal authority tells us who decides. It should not obscure who helped shape the conditions in which the decisions were made.
